# Can genome complexity date the origin of life? A calibrated test of the genome-complexity clock

**[Author names and affiliations]**

*Draft manuscript, 25 October 2026. Every number below is generated by the code in this repository
(`make reproduce-all`; tables in `results/RESULTS.md`). The pre-registered tests are specified in
`prereg/WP4_preregistration.md`, committed before the relevant data were examined.*

---

## Abstract

Sharov (2006) regressed the logarithm of functional genome size on the time of origin of five groups of
organisms and, extrapolating back to a single nucleotide, dated the origin of life to about 10 billion years
ago, before the Earth formed. Later work extended the dataset (Markov et al. 2010) and questioned the
statistics (Marzban et al. 2014), but the method itself has not been calibrated. We reproduce Sharov's
published regression exactly and show that within the straight-line model the pre-Earth date is
statistically firm (99% interval 6.5 to 22 Gya). The date is instead driven by an untestable assumption:
that complexity grew before the oldest data point at the same rate as after it. We then show three things.
First, statistics computed only from living species, such as the minimum genome size in each nested clade,
are blind to a uniform clock by construction and produce a log-linear trend with no clock at all, because
the extreme of a branching random walk advances linearly in time; in simulations with a known terrestrial
origin the method infers a pre-Earth origin in up to 100% of runs. Second, on 17,198 measured genomes and
the Timetree of Life, trendless models reproduce the observed "clock" slopes, different lineages imply
origins from 5.5 to 16.4 Gya, and the prokaryotic genome has barely grown since the last universal common
ancestor (LUCA). Third, in a pre-registered test using ancestral gene content from eggNOG 6, gene families
increase along the human, *Arabidopsis* and yeast lineages at about 0.19 log10 units per Gyr, but a constant
rate fails the registered linearity criterion and extrapolates to a single gene family 22.5 Gya, before the
Big Bang. Genome size and gene content therefore cannot date the origin of life. What the data do constrain
is the tempo of early evolution: a terrestrial origin requires the pre-LUCA genome to have doubled roughly
every 10 to 15 Myr.

---

## 1. Introduction

The idea that biological complexity grows at a measurable rate, and that the rate can be read backwards to
date the origin of life, is attractive because it would turn comparative genomics into a clock. Sharov (2006)
proposed that the functional, non-redundant genome of the most complex organisms of each era increased by
about 7.8-fold per billion years, and that, under a "strong exponential hypothesis", life originated about
10 Gya. Sharov and Gordon (2013) restated the estimate as 9.7 ± 2.5 Gya and argued for panspermia.

The proposal attracted open peer review that framed the main objections. Koonin argued that prokaryote genome
size shows no evidence of growth over the first 1.5 to 2 Gyr of life, and that a terrestrial origin should be
the null hypothesis. Adami argued that major organisational transitions should change the rate. Mushegian
agreed that early life appears "overloaded with evolutionary innovation", which asks for an explanation.
Markov, Anisimov and Korotayev (2010) compiled minimal genome sizes for nine nested groups on the lineage
leading to primates and found an accelerating (biexponential) trend, while cautioning that extrapolation was
"beyond the scope" of their paper. Marzban, Viswanathan and Yurtsever (2014) introduced measurement-error
models and prediction intervals and concluded that a terrestrial origin is consistent with the data.

Related proposals followed: a "C-value clock" (Li and Zhang 2010) and, recently, growth models fitted to
reconstructed ancestral genome sizes (Arroyo et al. 2025). Among about 170 works citing these papers, the
only substantive critique is Marzban et al.'s statistical one. None of this work asked whether the method
can recover a known answer. Here we (i) reproduce the published
analyses exactly; (ii) separate within-model from structural uncertainty; (iii) calibrate the method on
simulated histories where the origin is known; (iv) test it on modern data at the scale of thousands of
species; and (v) test the clock directly on the two data types that carry information about the past,
ancestral gene content and fossil genome-size proxies, under a pre-registered plan.

## 2. Methods

### 2.1 Published datasets and exact replication
Sharov (2006) gives no data table; values were taken from his text (Results) and ages read from his Fig. 1.
Eukaryotes at 2.05 Gya and mammals at 0.10 Gya reproduce all four of his printed statistics. Markov et al.'s
nine rows were verified against their Table 1. All values and their provenance are in `data/`.

### 2.2 Statistics on the published data
OLS with Fieller inverse-prediction intervals for the age at which the line reaches one base pair;
errors-in-variables fits (York 2004; Deming); the attenuation correction of Marzban et al.; small-sample AICc
comparisons of exponential, hyperbolic, biexponential and logistic forms; leave-one-out, segment fits and
backcasting; and current clade ages (Moody et al. 2024; Kay et al. 2025; dos Reis et al. 2015).

### 2.3 Calibration by simulation
Log genome size evolves as Brownian motion (optionally with drift, a reflecting floor, or extinction) on
birth-death trees rooted 4.0 Gya with a 1 Mb ancestor, so that the true origin is terrestrial. Markov's
construction (minimum over each ancestral clade of a focal extant species, regressed on clade age) and a
"most complex lineage" variant were applied to each simulated history. Coupled simulations (identical random
numbers with and without drift) test whether the construction responds to a true clock.

### 2.4 Real data
Directly measured genome sizes for 17,198 eukaryote species from Genomes on a Tree (GoaT), matched to the
2015 Timetree of Life (5,212 species on the tree) and NCBI Taxonomy; prokaryote genome sizes from GTDB R232
species representatives (CheckM2 completeness ≥ 95%, contamination ≤ 5%). Brownian and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck
rates were estimated by REML from independent contrasts (OU via the equivalent transformed tree). Trendless
nulls (Brownian, fitted OU, heavy-tailed increments, bounded) were simulated on the same pruned trees.

### 2.5 Pre-registered tests
Ancestral gene content: for each node on the human (16 nodes), *Arabidopsis* (7) and yeast (6) lineages, the
number of eggNOG 6 orthologous groups containing species on both sides of the node's basal split. Decision
rules P1 (log-linearity), P2 (backcasting), P4 (cross-lineage agreement), P5 (plausibility of the
extrapolated origin) and P6 (prokaryotic-era rate) were fixed in advance. Fossil genome sizes: decision
rules F1 to F3 on genome sizes estimated from fossil cell-size proxies.

### 2.6 Before LUCA
Monte Carlo over the LUCA age and genome size (Moody et al. 2024) and the onset of habitability gives the
average rate a terrestrial origin requires. Because post-LUCA data do not depend on the pre-LUCA rate, we
report the origin date implied by several priors on that rate.

## 3. Results

### 3.1 The published regression is reproducible, and within its own model the pre-Earth date is firm
Sharov's points give log10(y) = 8.64 + 0.89x (R² 0.97, 7.8-fold per Gyr) and an origin of 9.69 Gya, with
a 99% Fieller interval of 6.53 to 22.18 Gya. Markov et al.'s published "R² = 0.914" is Pearson's r; R² is
0.836. Under the repository's own error bars the straight line is rejected for Markov's nine points (York
χ² = 47.4 on 7 df, p = 4.7 × 10⁻⁸), and Markov's preferred biexponential fits better (AICc −9.5 vs −4.1)
while levelling off near 10⁶ bp, with no origin at all. Updating clade ages lowers R² to 0.74 and moves the
straight-line origin to 11.8 Gya.

### 3.2 The date is set by an assumption the data cannot test
Fitting only the Phanerozoic points gives an origin of 3.8 Gya; fitting only the Precambrian points gives
18.3 Gya. Any extrapolation equals the first point's age plus its log size divided by the early rate, so the
inferred origin is the push-forward of whatever is assumed about that rate (Fig. `early_rate`). Measurement
error cannot rescue a terrestrial point estimate unless every clade age carries about 1 Gyr of error. We
could not reproduce Marzban et al.'s prediction bands from their printed equations (Section 3.8).

### 3.3 Living-species statistics cannot see a clock, and report one when there is none
In coupled simulations, adding a uniform clock of +0.8 log10 per Gyr leaves the nested-minimum slope
unchanged to machine precision (0.516 in both runs), because every living genome carries the same
accumulated growth; the true ancestral series changes by exactly 0.8. With no clock at all, the
construction returns positive slopes with R² of about 0.9, and infers a pre-Earth origin in 16% to 100% of
runs depending on parameters, and in 88% to 100% for settings that reproduce Markov's observed slope.
Selecting the most complex living lineage, as Sharov did, biases even its true ancestral series upward
(0.25 to 1.65 log10 per Gyr with no clock).

### 3.4 Real data behave like a trendless process
Rebuilding Markov's table from 17,198 measured genomes reproduces his minima closely, but the implied rate
depends on the statistic: 1.63 log10 per Gyr for the clade minimum, 1.00 for the 1st percentile and 0.19
for the median (R² 0.53). Across 2,362 animal species used as focal lineages, the observed rate (median 1.56,
R² 0.89) lies within the range produced by every trendless null on the same tree. In plants, OU fits far
better than Brownian motion (ΔAIC 178; half-life about 110 Myr), and the fitted OU reproduces the observed
rate (1.41 vs 1.31). Different lineages imply different origins: 5.5 Gya from mammals, 6.0 from animals,
7.8 from plants, 8.3 from arthropods and 16.4 from fungi.

### 3.5 The prokaryotic genome has barely grown since LUCA
Among 36,268 high-quality prokaryote isolate species (GTDB R232), the median genome is 4.31 Mb, and 13% to
21% are smaller than LUCA's estimated 2.49 to 2.99 Mb (65% to 76% of all archaeal species). Growth from LUCA
to the median modern isolate implies 0.056 log10 per Gyr, about 16 times slower than Sharov's rate,
consistent with Koonin's stasis argument.

### 3.6 Pre-registered test: ancestral gene content
LUCA is inferred to have carried 2,728 gene families, close to Moody et al.'s independent estimate of 2,657
proteins (2,451 to 2,855). Our LECA estimate (8,514 families) lies between earlier estimates of about 4,100
genes (Koonin 2010) and 10,233 families (Vosseberg et al. 2021). The steep early accumulation agrees with
phylostratigraphy, where about 60% of human genes date to the origin of cellular life or of eukaryotes
(Domazet-Lošo and Tautz 2008). Along the human lineage, ancestral families rise to 8,514 at LECA and to roughly 15,000 to
20,000 in mammals and primates. The rate is 0.188 log10 per Gyr (95% CI 0.129 to 0.247), similar for
*Arabidopsis* (0.166) and yeast (0.169). By the pre-registered rules the clock is not supported: log-linearity
fails (R² 0.77 < 0.80) and a constant rate extrapolates to one gene family 22.5 Gya, before the Big Bang.
Backcasting, cross-lineage agreement and the prokaryotic-era rate pass. The verdict is unchanged with a
second statistic, with literature node ages, and in an exploratory subset restricted to well-sampled nodes.

### 3.8 Before LUCA, and a reproduction of Marzban et al.
A terrestrial origin requires an average rate 34 times Sharov's from a single nucleotide (95% range 20 to 97),
or 23 times from a 100-nucleotide replicator: a genome doubling every 10 to 15 Myr. The probability that the
origin lies on Earth is 0 under Sharov's assumption of a constant rate, 0.22 under a log-uniform prior on the
early rate spanning 0.1 to 100 times the fitted rate, and 0.56 if early evolution may have been 1 to 1000
times faster; the data cannot move these numbers. Applying Marzban et al.'s equations as printed, their
ordinary prediction band reaches one base pair at 8.15 Gya (7.43 with a t-quantile) rather than the 7.0
shown, and the λ = 1.14 band at 5.6 rather than 4.5 Gya.

## 4. Discussion

**What the clock was really measuring.** The regularity Sharov and Markov found is real, but it is a property
of how the points were chosen, not of how genomes evolved. Minimum or leading-edge genomes of nested clades
form a log-linear series under any process that spreads genome sizes out across a diversifying tree, and a
uniform directional trend leaves no trace in such data. This is a general caution for any "complexity
clock" built from living representatives.

**Relation to previous work.** That extreme values can masquerade as trends is an old insight in
palaeobiology (Gould 1988; McShea 1994). Trammer (2005) found that maximum body size tracks diversification,
scaling roughly with the square root of the diversification rate, which matches the speed σ√(2r) of a
branching random walk (Hammersley 1974; Biggins 1977; Bramson 1978). Cladogenetic diffusion models explain
the shapes of body-size distributions without a drive (Clauset and Erwin 2008), although large directional
increases can exceed what neutral drift produces (Heim et al. 2015). That a trend uniform in time cannot be
estimated from contemporaneous tips of an ultrametric tree is known in comparative methods: the likelihood
surface is flat with respect to the trend (Pennell et al. 2014; Gill et al. 2017), and fossils are needed to
recover it (Slater et al. 2012; Hunt and Slater 2016; Finarelli and Flynn 2006). Selecting large or
successful clades biases inferences about their past (Budd and Mann 2018, 2020). What is new here is
bringing these strands together for complexity clocks: an exact demonstration that a uniform clock is
invisible to clade-minimum and leading-edge statistics; the link between the fitted "rate" and trait
variance and diversification; calibration on real trees; and a pre-registered test on ancestral gene
content. Trends that vary among branches can be detected from living species with appropriate models (Baker
et al. 2015; Gill et al. 2017). Testing whether particular lineages show driven increases in complexity is a
natural next step, but it is a different hypothesis from a universal clock.

**What the data do say.** The direct evidence about the past points the other way. Gene content in ancestors
grows, but slowly, and a constant rate is physically impossible when extrapolated. The prokaryotic genome
shows near-stasis since LUCA. Complexity therefore appears to have risen in bursts tied to major transitions,
with a rapid start: LUCA was already a cell with about 2,700 gene families.

**Life before Earth.** Nothing here rules out panspermia, which must be judged on astrophysical and
geochemical grounds. Our results say only that genome size and gene content provide no evidence for it. The
interesting quantitative question that remains is how fast pre-LUCA evolution was. A doubling of genome
content every 10 to 15 Myr is far faster than any sustained rate observed since, but well within the reach
of processes such as horizontal transfer-dominated communal evolution (Vetsigian, Woese and Goldenfeld 2006)
and gene duplication, which can double a genome in one generation.

**Limitations.** Genome size is an imperfect proxy for functional complexity; eggNOG orthogroup counts depend
on clustering granularity and outgroup sampling; homology detection weakens with depth; the 2015 Timetree is
not the latest version (TimeTree 6 covers only some groups); our simulated nulls are simple. Each of these
would make ancestral content look smaller at deep nodes and therefore favour the clock, which nonetheless
fails.

## 5. Data and code availability

All code, curated data and derived results are at https://github.com/itsbakr/dna-before-earth
(branch `claude/review-critique-plan`). External datasets (GoaT, TimeTree, NCBI Taxonomy, GTDB, eggNOG) are
downloaded by `scripts/fetch_data.py` with checksums; TimeTree data are not redistributed, in line with its
terms.
